stories.title: Agility Robotics closes first Nasdaq day up after SPAC debut
paragraphs: The Robot Report says Agility Robotics began trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 5, 2026, under ticker AGLT after completing its merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, calling itself the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public. Shares opened at $11.26 versus the $10 SPAC deal price.

According to the report's day-one wrap, AGLT traded as low as $8.40 and as high as $12.15 before closing at $11.49, about 2% above the open, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%. The earlier listing story said gross proceeds were about $465 million before expenses.

Agility says Digit has logged more than 65,000 operating hours across customer sites and claims more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders for Digit 5, with early-access deliveries expected in 2027. CEO Peggy Johnson has discussed possible additional form factors beyond the current Digit lineup.

stories.title: Serve Robotics launches Physical AI Services to sell robot connectivity and data tools
paragraphs: TechCrunch reports that Serve Robotics, the public sidewalk-delivery robot maker that spun out of Uber's Postmates acquisition, announced a new Physical AI Services business on Nov. 5, 2026, alongside third-quarter earnings, aiming to sell technology it built for its own fleets to other robot developers.

According to CEO Ali Kashani, the line includes Serve Link for connecting field robots to data-center AI over unreliable networks, a data curator for finding edge cases in robot logs, and a foundation-model data catalog drawn from Serve's sidewalk robots. Bedrock Robotics is named as a customer, and Serve is also working with T-Mobile on bringing AI compute closer to robots.

Kashani told TechCrunch the company is keeping its delivery and hospital-robot businesses while opening the stack so others can build on it, comparing the move to Amazon's AWS moment after running the technology end-to-end itself first.

stories.title: Boston Dynamics unveils Stretch Gen 2 for faster trailer unloading and repairs
paragraphs: Boston Dynamics announced Stretch Gen 2 on Nov. 3, 2026, as the next generation of its autonomous mobile trailer-unloading robot. RoboticsTomorrow reports the redesign draws on more than 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes unloaded by first-generation Stretch to cut unplanned downtime.

According to the company release carried by RoboticsTomorrow, Gen 2 uses automotive-grade connectors, an upgraded gripper with finer sensing, continuous-rotation joints that no longer hit hard stops, and about 81% less internal cabling—removing a major source of electrical faults. Exterior panels and a recessed emergency stop are meant to reduce accidental stoppages from falling boxes.

Boston Dynamics says a full swerve-drive swap now takes about one hour instead of a full day, and onboard diagnostics aim to let customer teams handle more routine service. Stretch Gen 2 can unload up to 1,000 cases per hour depending on case weight and stacking, runs about two shifts per charge, and fast-charges to 90% in about 75 minutes.

stories.title: Hopcopter's flexible foot pad steadies hopping landings across rough terrain
paragraphs: New Atlas reports that researchers at City University of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, and the University of Toronto upgraded the bird-inspired Hopcopter—a quadcopter with one spring-loaded hopping leg—with a flexible foot pad for ice, sand, rocks, and slopes.

According to New Atlas, the wider pad spreads weight to limit sinking, rubber bands help the foot recenter after impact, and short spikes improve grip on slippery surfaces. The team says the pad cut performance variation across terrains by 84% compared with the earlier flat-surface prototype.

New Atlas notes hopping uses brief rotor bursts after free-fall and can use about one-tenth the energy of continuous flight for the same-size drone. A paper appears in Advanced Intelligent Systems; partners are commercializing a Hop-1 version and exploring AI obstacle avoidance for search-and-rescue and inspection roles.
